region.en: Angeles, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省安赫勒斯（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20a 'How Salaksak became Rich', eBook #8299

summary.en: Jealous Salaksak baits his brother Cucunu: a cow killed for trespassing becomes a thousand-peso claim on innocent herdsmen; a sack of ashes from his burned house is swapped with an old man's money-bag on the road; when Cucunu cages him by the river, Salaksak cries that he is imprisoned for refusing the ruler's daughter, is freed by a suitor with a herd of cows, and finally drowns his envious brother with the tale that their dead parents keep cows under the sea.
summary.zh: 薩拉克薩克步步設局：越界的牛被兄長殺死，他反以牛皮向無辜牧人索賠千金；燒屋後的灰燼在路途上換取老人背著的銀錢袋；被兄長關進河邊籠中時，他哭喊『因拒娶官家之女而囚』，被求婚者以牛群贖出。最後他謊稱海底有亡父亡母養著牛群，妒火中燒的兄長縱身入河，一去不返。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan droll recorded by Fansler from a Licup narrator (Angeles); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F4BE1HJ).

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived two brothers, the elder named Cucunu and the younger Salaksak, their parents dead; each received a cow and a piece of land, and Salaksak built a small house of his own. Jealous because his brother's rice grew faster than his own, Salaksak one night turned his cow loose in Cucunu's field; when it happened again the impatient brother killed the cow, and Salaksak, ashamed and afraid, took only the skin and put it into a basket. Not long afterward several hundred cows passed him along the road; while the herdsmen were eating their dinner he threw his skin among the cows, then asked the chief of the herdsmen to count them, since his cow had been lost a week and might have become mixed with the herd. As the chief counted, Salaksak picked up the skin and shook his head: 'Alas! Here is the mark of my cow... You must pay me a thousand pesos, or else you shall be imprisoned. My cow was easily worth a thousand pesos; for when she was alive, she used to drop money every day.' In their great fear the herdsmen paid him at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Salaksak went home and told his brother of his good fortune; hoping to become as rich as his brother, Cucunu immediately killed his own cow — and was summoned by the ruler of the town, accused of having stolen the hide, and whipped so badly that he could hardly walk home. Maddened by the disgrace, Cucunu burned his brother's house while he was away; when Salaksak came home to find nothing but ashes, he put them into a sack and set out to seek his fortune again. On the way he overtook an old man carrying a bag of money to the ruler's house, and said, 'I am sorry for you, old man. What do you say to exchanging loads? Mine is very light in comparison with yours.' 'With all my heart, kind boy!' — and they exchanged sacks; at a safe hiding-place Salaksak deserted his companion and went to tell his brother he had gotten a sack of silver for a sack of ashes. 'Why, my house is bigger than yours! I ought to get two sacks of ashes if I burn it. I think that would be a good bargain.' So Cucunu burned his house too, and went through the town crying, 'Who wants to buy ashes?' — until the ruler, remembering him, summoned him and lashed him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Thoroughly enraged, Cucunu determined his brother should not deceive him a third time: he made a strong cage, caught Salaksak, and confined him in it by the bank of the river — 'I will give you three days to repent. Now you cannot deceive me any more.' As a young man was passing by, Salaksak began to cry out, 'They have put me into this cage because I do not want to marry the ruler's daughter.' The young man, who had vainly striven for the hand of the girl, immediately approached: 'If you will let me take your place, so that I may marry her, I will give you all the cows I have with me.' So by this trick Salaksak escaped, while Cucunu, thinking the man in the cage was his brother, unmercifully threw him into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A few days later Salaksak went to his brother's house and told him it was quite beautiful under the water: 'There I saw our father and mother. They told me I was not old enough to stay with them, so they sent me back here with a large number of cows.' 'Well, well!' said Cucunu, 'I too must go see our parents.' He then hastened to the river, threw himself in, and was drowned. Thus Salaksak grew rich because of his craftiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 聰明的胡安與嫉妒的迭戈

region.en: Santa Maria, Bulakan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋布拉克省聖瑪麗亞（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20b 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego', eBook #8299

summary.en: Juan stage-manages his own mother's 'death' and revival with a bamboo tube; the thieving Diego tries the trick at a child's funeral and is kicked away. Left the thin carabao, Juan sells the hide by dropping it on bandits from a tree and looting their treasure; boxed for the sea by Diego, he swaps places with a gold-ring peddler and later drowns his brother with the tale of a mother beneath the waves giving away gold rings.
summary.zh: 胡安導演母親『死而復生』；迭戈竊管到喪禮上故技重施，反被踢走。分得瘦水牛的胡安以牛皮自樹上砸退匪幫、席捲其財寶；被迭戈装箱投海前，他與賣金戒指的中國小販調包。歸來後他謊稱海底的母親正以金戒指相贈——愚兄欣然下海，再未浮起。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from an Anzures narrator (story from Santa Maria, Bulakan); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes G1F5HJ).

passages.text: There were once two brothers named Diego and Juan whose father had died long before, so they lived only with their good mother; Diego, the older, was envious and foolish, Juan was clever. One morning Juan called his mother: 'Mother, help me fool Diego! Please lie down as if you were dead; and when he arrives, I will blow air through your nose through a bamboo tube. As soon as you feel me blowing, get up and try to look like a woman that has risen from the dead.' When Diego came in and saw his brother crying, 'Don't you see? Our mother is dead,' Juan opened his trunk, took out a short bamboo tube, and blew through it into his mother's nose — and she pretended to revive. Diego rejoiced, very much surprised at his brother's possession.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the envious Diego stole the bamboo tube and went to the churchyard, where he waited for a funeral. When the procession of a small boy came along he stopped it, and called to the mother of the boy, 'Don't cry! Your son is only sleeping. Lay him down here, and you will soon see that he is alive.' After opening the coffin he began to blow air into the boy's nose, blowing harder and harder — but the boy remained as stiff and lifeless as ever, and the angry mother kicked Diego, saying, 'You are only trying to fool us!' Diego was very much ashamed, so he threw away the bamboo tube and ran home. Some days later the mother of Diego and Juan became ill and died, leaving her sons two carabaos: Diego took the fat one, Juan the thin one — and Juan, angry, killed his carabao and set out to sell the hide.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finding no buyer in the neighboring villages, Juan walked on until he came to a forest, and climbing a tree hid himself with his hide among the branches — for a band of Tulisanes on horseback with a large amount of treasure was coming toward him. They stopped to eat under that very tree; Juan unintentionally moved the hide on the branch beside him, and it fell crashing down on the Tulisanes, who, frightened by this most unexpected noise, ran away as fast as they could, not stopping to take anything with them. Juan descended quickly, mounted a horse, and made off with as much as he could carry. When Diego heard that the riches had been given by the neighboring villages in return for the carabao-hide, he went out and killed his fat carabao, dried its hide, and tried to sell it in the villages — but many days passed and still no one would buy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now Diego was very angry. He took a wooden box and put his brother inside, bound it, and carried it to the seashore — but remembering that it was not locked, he left it and went back to the house for the key. Meanwhile a Chinese peddler selling gold rings came along, and Juan shouted, 'Chino, Chino, come and see these beautiful and precious things inside!' The Chinaman approached and opened the box, and Juan came out, saying, 'I will put you inside, and you will see many beautiful things in the bottom'; the willing Chino was shut in, and Juan took the gold rings and ran away. Not many minutes later Diego came up, locked the box, and threw it into the ocean. That same day, while Diego was eating his dinner, Juan came along with some fine gold rings; asked how he had escaped and where the rings came from, Juan answered that he had sunk to the bottom of the ocean, where he saw his mother, and that she had given him all those rings. The foolish Diego believed everything, and asked his brother to put him into a box and throw him into the ocean; Juan lost no time in obeying, and after that lived happily for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.

region.en: Jaen, Nueva Ecija, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋新怡詩夏省哈恩（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20c 'Ruined because of Invidiousness', eBook #8299

summary.en: Poor Juan plants his cow-hide in a butcher's piles and extorts five hundred pesos 'or else a lawsuit'; climbing a tree at a crossroads, he drops the hide on armed men who flee believing it a curse from heaven, leaving sacks of money. Returning his brother's borrowed salop with coins stuck in the cracks, he lets Pedro conclude that one hide is worth two sacks of money — and the envious brother slaughters his whole herd for hides no one will buy.
summary.zh: 窮漢胡安把牛皮混入肉鋪皮堆，訛得五百比索『否則告官』；又在十字路口樹上將牛皮砸落武裝匪徒頭頂——匪徒以為天罰，棄錢囊而逃。歸還兄長的量米斗時，他把銀幣嵌進斗縫，令佩德羅相信『一張皮值兩袋錢』——妒火中燒的兄長宰盡牛群，製成的皮卻無人問津。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from an Esquivel narrator (Jaen, Nueva Ecija); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F4F5F6).

passages.text: In time out of memory there lived two brothers, Pedro and Juan: Pedro was rich, for he had a large herd of cattle, and had not much use for his younger brother, who was very poor. Juan had nothing he could call his own but a cow; one day, disappointed over his life of poverty, he killed his cow and set out to find his fortune with nothing but the hide. When he reached the next town he saw large piles of cattle-hides in front of a butcher's shop, and late that night he stole out secretly and put the skin of his cow in one of the piles. The next morning he went to the shop: 'Mr.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Butcher, I have come here to look for my lost cow. Have you not killed a cow with a mark J on the right hip?' 'No, all the cows which were killed here came from my herd out there in the mountains,' answered the honest man — until, searching the piles, they found the hide Juan had put there, and Juan began to quarrel: 'You must pay me five hundred pesos for my cow, or else I shall bring a law-suit before the court against you. You stole my cow, and now you have to pay for it.' The man, very much afraid of being brought before the court, gave Juan the five hundred pesos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way home he came to a tree standing at a cross-roads; very tired and thirsty, he climbed it to look for a house, but instead of a house he saw a company of armed men coming down the road, who stopped under the tree to rest. Juan was so terrified that he hardly knew what to do; as he was trembling with fright, the hide fell down from the tree and frightened the men away — they thought it was a curse from heaven because of their misdeeds. When Juan realized the men were gone he quickly descended, and there on the ground he saw a number of sacks full of money; loading a horse with two of the sacks, he started for his home town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as he reached his house he went to his brother's to borrow a salop, inserted several pesetas and ten-centavo pieces in the cracks of the measure, and returned it. 'What did you do with the salop?' asked Pedro, seeing the coins sticking in the cracks. 'I measured money,' said Juan. 'Where did you get the money?' 'Don't you know that I went to the neighboring town to sell my cowhide? Just think! One hide is worth two sacks of money.' Pedro, who was envious of his brother's good fortune, killed all his cattle, old and young, and threw the meat into the river; then he started with several carretons full of hides — but he was disappointed, for nobody would buy hides. Discouraged and tired out, he returned to find Juan living comfortably in a fine new home: thus Pedro lost all his property because of his invidiousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Friends: The Enchanted Hide and the Mother's Corpse
title.zh: 兩位朋友：『魔皮』與母親的屔體

region.zh: 菲律賓怡朗省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Filipino oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20d 'The Two Friends', eBook #8299

summary.en: Small, poor Andres outwits his rich, strong friend Juan again and again: watching through the floor of an adulterous house, he sells the husband an 'enchanted hide' that reveals a man in the trunk and fish in the cupboard; he sells his dead mother's corpse to a terrified doctor; and when Juan sacks him for the sea, the cowboy who 'willingly marries the king's daughter' takes his place — until the envious Juan dives after 'cows from under the sea' himself.
summary.zh: 瘦弱的安德烈斯屢屢戲弄富有的強壯朋友胡安：隔著屋板目睹偷情場面後，他把『能召人召魚的魔皮』高價賣給丈夫；他又把亡母屔體賣給驚惶的醫生。被胡安裝袋投海時，牛倌自稱『願娶國王之女』而代其受溺。最後妒火中燒的胡安，聽說海底有牛群，也自己跳了下去。

sensitivity.note: Filipino droll recorded by Fansler from a Vargas narrator (possibly of Iloilo); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F2G2HJ).

passages.text: Once there lived in a certain village two friends, Juan and Andres: Juan, a very rich man, was tall, big, and strong, while Andres, a very poor man, was small, weak, and short; Andres worked very hard to earn his living, while Juan spent most of his time on pleasure. One morning Andres borrowed one of Juan's mules, promising to tell the truth if anyone asked who owned it — but when two neighbors asked where he got it, he said he had bought it, and the news spreading, Juan angrily ordered the mule brought back. A week later two of Juan's mules, including the one Andres had borrowed, died; Juan threw the carcasses away, but Andres took the skins and dried them to sell in the next town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Overtaken by night near a solitary house between his village and the town, Andres asked a woman for lodging, and had to wait until her husband came; from where he sat he could see that the woman was preparing a good supper for a stranger who meanwhile had entered — and when another man approached in the distance, the woman hastily opened a big empty trunk and hid the first man inside, putting all the cooked fish in the cupboard. When the husband arrived and received him kindly, Andres told him at the supperless table that he had an enchanted hide: 'I ordered the skin to bring a man into the trunk; and when the trunk was opened, there was the man. Next I ordered the skin to bring cooked fish to the cupboard; and when the cupboard was opened, there was the cooked fish.' The husband then offered Andres a very high price for the enchanted skin, and Andres willingly sold it — early the next morning leaving the house before the others were up, and returning to the village rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Juan noticed the money in his friend's pocket, Andres told him it was the price of the skins of his dead mules, which he had sold in the neighboring town — and Juan went directly home, killed all his mules, and flayed them. Passing the solitary house crying that he had skins for sale, he was taken for the same man who had sold the enchanted skin, and the husband whipped him nearly to death. Determined to kill his friend, Juan finally caught Andres — but Andres was very cunning and avoided him — and in his anger killed the mother of Andres. When Andres found his mother dead, he dressed her very well and took her to town, explaining definitely her sickness to the town doctor; but just after she had been given the medicine the doctor noticed that the woman was dead, and Andres accused him of having poisoned his mother: the doctor, fearing the consequences if Andres should seek justice, agreed to pay him a large sum of money.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Andres returned to his village richer than ever, and Juan became friendly again, asking where he had gotten his money: 'It was the price of my mother's corpse, which I sold in the town.' Juan went home and killed his mother; but taking the corpse to town to sell it, he was abused by a crowd of men and narrowly escaped with his life. Now determined not to let Andres escape him, Juan one day caught him, put him inside a sack, and carried it down to the seashore — going to a house on the way to get a light for a smoke. Meanwhile Andres, bound in the sack, was crying out that he did not wish to marry the daughter of the king, and was being forced against his will; a cowboy with his herd of cows passed by, heard him, and said he was willing to marry the king's daughter — so Andres had him unbind the sack, put the cowherd in his stead, and hurried away with the cows. Juan came back, picked up the sack, and threw it into the sea; when he returned home he found Andres there with a fine herd of cows, which Andres said he had gotten from under the sea. So Juan, envious as ever, ordered Andres to put him in a sack and throw him into the sea — and Andres gladly did so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Orphan: The Sirena Awaits

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20e 'Juan the Orphan', eBook #8299

summary.en: Envious Uncle Diego kills Juan's only horse; Juan trades the horse-meat to a starving old man for his sack of money, and Diego, slaughtering all fifteen of his own horses, finds buyers only laugh at his asking price of 'three hundred ninety-nine thousand pesos, ninety-nine pesetas, six and one half centavos a pound.' Sacking the orphan for the river, he finds him back next morning 'returning to my love the Sirena' — and pleads to go first, tied in the rice-sack himself.
summary.zh: 嫉妒的叔叔迭戈殺了孤兒胡安唯一的馬；胡安以馬肉換得老人的錢袋。迭戈宰盡自家十五匹馬叫賣，開價『三十九萬九千九百九十九比索零九十九仙六分半一磅』，只惹來哄笑。他把胡安縫入麻袋準備投河，翌日卻見胡安笑著回來——『我要回到河底，我的人魚愛人在等我』——叔叔苦求先去，親手讓自己被縛入米袋。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F4H-modified J); the Sirena is the Philippine mermaid.

passages.text: There once lived a boy whose name was Juan; his parents had died, leaving him nothing but a horse, which he begged his Uncle Diego to let stay in his stable, feeding it from time to time and caring for it as a father would for a son. One day Uncle Diego noticed that Juan's horse was growing fatter and more beautiful than any of his own animals, and in his envy he killed the horse of his nephew, telling the innocent boy that the animal had been stricken by 'bad air.' Being thus deprived of his sole wealth, Juan cut off the best meat from the dead horse, and with this food for his only provision set out to seek his fortune in another country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way through a forest he came across an old man dying of starvation, but with a bag full of money. 'Pray, what have you in your sack, my son?' 'Some dried horse-meat,' said Juan. 'Will you exchange your sack of meat for my sack of money? I have money here, but I cannot eat it... Since you are stronger, my son, pray take this sack of money in exchange, and go to the town and buy meat with it for yourself. For God's sake, leave this meat to me! I am starving to death.' Juan accepted the money, put the heavy bag on his shoulder, and with difficulty carried it home — 'I sold the meat of my dead horse. This is what I got for it,' he told his uncle, who once more became jealous: 'If with only one horse he could gain so much money, how much should I get for my fifteen horses!' So he killed all the horses he had in his stable and cut the meat from them; then he placed the meat in bags, and crying as he went along the street, 'Meat, meat! Horse-meat! Who wishes to buy fresh horse-meat?' answered the gray-headed old woman who asked the price: 'Three hundred ninety-nine thousand pesos, ninety-nine pesetas, six and one half centavos a pound,' said Uncle Diego. The people who heard him only laughed, and thought something was the matter with his head; nobody would buy his meat, and all his meat decayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He went home in despair and planned to take vengeance on his nephew: he cast the little orphan into a big sack and sewed the mouth of the little prison all up, saying that at night he would take the sack and throw it into the river. However, Juan managed to get out of the bag, and in his place put a muzzled dog; when night came the uncle shouldered the bag, took it to the river, and hurled it into the deep water. But when morning came, Uncle Diego saw Juan smilingly enter the door of his house: 'I haven't time; there is not a moment to lose. I have only come here to bid you good-by. Back to the bottom of the river. My love, the Sirena, is waiting for me.' 'O Juan! If I could only go with you!' — 'No, no, no!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Only one can go at a time. The Sirena would be angry, and she would consequently refuse to admit to her glorious habitation any being from this outside world.' But the uncle pleaded so earnestly that finally the boy yielded with pretended reluctance; the uncle then covered himself with a rice-sack, and Juan tied the mouth of the bag securely. 'I will fool him,' Uncle Diego said to himself. 'I will fool him,' Juan said to himself. 'There is no such thing as the Sirena in the river. Thank God, my dreadful uncle will soon be disposed of!' At midnight Juan hurled his happy uncle into the river, saying, 'There is no one who owes that must not pay his debt. May my act be justified!' The heavy sack sank to the bottom of the river, and nothing more was heard of Uncle Diego.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.
